text.p: Most of Japan's five major steelmakers Thursday reported profit gains for last year, helped mainly by cost-cutting and partly by a weak yen.
The group also expects better profits in the current year.

The nation's top steelmaker, Nippon Steel, said its parent current profit in the year to March 1997 rose 30.9 percent from a year earlier to 84.71 billion yen ($730 million), helped by cost-cutting efforts.
But Kobe Steel's profits slipped in the last business year and Kobe and NKK forecast flat profits in the current year.
Nippon Steel predicted parent current profit of 100 billion yen ($862 million) for 1997/98.

Japanese steelmakers are seeking a rise in prices paid by large customers, having cut prices over the last five years amid the appreciation of the yen against the dollar. The supply/demand balance for steel is tight in Asia, but an increase in production capacity in South Korea and Taiwan is expected to have an impact on Japan's export prices later in the year, steelmakers said.

Sumitomo Metal Industries said its parent current profit rose 10.8 percent from a year earlier to 22.43 billion yen ($193 million) in 1996/97, mainly helped by cost-cutting and partly by the weak yen. Vice president Kazuaki Tsuda said it expects 1997/98 parent current profit to rise to 30 billion yen ($258 million), mainly due to cost-cutting.
The average yen/dollar rate stood at about 113 yen in 1996/97 against 96 yen a year earlier. Steelmakers assume an average yen/dollar rate between 115 and 120 yen for 1997/98.

Kawasaki Steel Corp. posted a 41.8 percent year-on-year gain in its 1996/97 parent current profit to 23.58 billion yen ($203 million) and forecast a 1997/98 current profit of 38 billion yen ($327 million)
"We expect the domestic selling price to rise slightly (due to tight supplies). We really want to raise the selling price for large-lot customers," Kawasaki Steel vice president Koichi Masuda said.
NKK's parent current profit rose 13 percent to 34.27 billion yen ($295 million) in 1996/97, helped by the weak yen, despite lower profits in its engineering division.

It predicted current profit in 1997/98 would be almost flat at 34 billion yen ($293 million), achieved by cost-cutting and a rise in prices for large customers. It expects a 4.6 percent decline in 1997/98 parent sales mainly due to poor sales in its engineering division.

Kobe Steel said its parent current profit fell 26 percent from a year earlier to 26.67 billion yen ($229 million), due to lower selling prices of steel and aluminum and worse profits in its machinery division. It forecast almost flat parent current profit of 27 billion yen ($232 million) for 1997/98.
The five Japanese major steelmakers expect Japan's overall crude steel production to be about 100 million tons in 1997/98, little changed from 100.8 million tons.
